mercy_translation.text:
Because of these things, death gained ever greater power and corruption remained against humanity. The human race was being corrupted; the rational human being, made according to the image, was disappearing; and the work made by God was being destroyed.

For, as I said before, death now had the force of law against us, and it was not possible simply to escape that law, since God had established it because of the transgression. What was happening was therefore at once truly unreasonable and unfitting.

It would have been unreasonable for God, having spoken, to prove false: after he had laid down that the human being would die if he transgressed the commandment, it could not be that after the transgression the human being would not die and God's word be annulled. God would not be truthful if, after he had said that we would die, the human being did not die.

But it would also have been unfitting that beings once made rational and having participated in his Word should perish and return again to non-being through corruption.

For it was not worthy of the goodness of God that the things made by him should be destroyed because of the deception brought upon human beings by the devil.

Moreover, it was most unfitting that God's workmanship in human beings should disappear either through their own negligence or through the deceit of demons.

Since rational beings were being corrupted and works of this kind were perishing, what was God, being good, to do? Was he to allow corruption to prevail over them and death to hold them? And what need would there have been for them to be made in the first place? It would have been better not to have been made than, once made, to be neglected and perish.

Neglect would reveal weakness rather than goodness in God if, after making his work, he looked on while it was corrupted—more so than if he had never made the human being at the beginning.

For if he had not made humanity, there would have been no one to consider such weakness. But once he had made and created them into being, it would have been utterly unreasonable for the works to perish, especially before the eyes of the One who made them.

Therefore human beings could not simply be left to be carried away by corruption, for this would be unfitting and unworthy of the goodness of God.

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
Athanasius sets up a theological dilemma: God's truthfulness and God's goodness must both be upheld.
The repeated language of what is 'fitting' or 'unfitting' expresses Athanasius' theological reasoning from God's character.
